subject: Banking
title: Banking as a Service
description: A quick, practical guide to Banking as a Service.

hook.text: Shopify offers business bank accounts. Uber has a debit card. Neither is a bank.

buildup.text: BaaS companies like Synapse and Unit provide banking infrastructure through APIs.

discovery.text: A licensed bank sits behind the scenes holding deposits and ensuring compliance.

twist.text: Synapse collapsed in 2024, freezing millions in customer funds.

climax.text: BaaS promised anyone could become a bank. Reality showed that banking requires stability.

punchline.text: Any company can offer banking. But banking requires trust that is hard to build.

quiz.question: What happened when BaaS provider Synapse collapsed?
options: Millions in customer funds were frozen because the middleware layer failed

details.summary: Banking as a service allows non-bank companies to offer financial products like accounts, cards, and loans by connecting to licensed banks through APIs, without obtaining their own banking license or building infrastructure from scratch.
details.whyItMatters: BaaS lets any company embed banking into its product. A ride-sharing app can offer driver bank accounts, or a retailer can issue branded credit cards, all powered by a bank operating invisibly in the background.
takeaways: Non-bank companies offer banking products via licensed bank partners
The bank provides licensing, compliance, and infrastructure behind the scenes
BaaS revenue is growing as embedded finance becomes mainstream

faq.question: Who is responsible if something goes wrong with a BaaS product?
faq.answer: The licensed sponsor bank retains ultimate regulatory responsibility. This has caused problems when fintech partners took risks the bank failed to oversee. Regulators have increased scrutiny of sponsor bank partnerships after several failures.

faq.question: Can any company offer banking services through BaaS?
faq.answer: Technically, any company can embed financial products through a BaaS provider. But sponsor banks conduct due diligence on partners, and regulators are tightening standards. Companies must meet compliance requirements even without their own license.
